paragraphs.title: Legislated Injustice and the Day of Judgment

easy.explanation: The passage begins, “Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees.”
easy.q: Whom does the prophet condemn in these verses?

answers: The needy, the poor, widows, and the fatherless
easy.explanation: The passage names the needy, the poor, widows, and the fatherless as victims.
easy.q: Who suffers injustice according to these verses?

easy.explanation: The prophet warns of “the day of visitation” and “the desolation which shall come from far.”
easy.q: What will come in the day of visitation?

answers: They have perverted judgment and oppressed the weak
medium.explanation: Their own decrees turned aside the needy and robbed the poor, widows, and fatherless.
medium.q: Why will the unjust rulers have difficulty escaping in the day of visitation?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to laws that institutionalize injustice and oppression.
medium.q: What does the phrase “unrighteous decrees” mean?

answers: “To whom will ye flee for help?”
medium.explanation: The prophet asks, “To whom will ye flee for help?”
medium.q: What question shows the oppressors' lack of refuge?

answers: The laws were designed to protect them
The laws allowed them to be exploited
The laws had nothing to do with them
challenge.explanation: The rulers made widows their prey and robbed the fatherless.
challenge.q: What connection is made between the rulers' laws and widows and orphans?

answers: The oppressors will lose their status and security
They will willingly give away their honor
challenge.explanation: Their wealth, position, and glory will not protect them in the day of judgment.
challenge.q: What does “where will ye leave your glory?” imply?

answers: God's anger continues and His hand remains stretched out
challenge.explanation: The passage says, “For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.”
challenge.q: What is emphasized at the end of the passage?

paragraphs.title: Assyria as an Instrument of Punishment and the Conqueror's Pride

easy.explanation: The Lord addresses Assyria as “the rod of mine anger.”
easy.q: Who is called “the rod of mine anger”?

answers: To punish, plunder, and oppress a sinful people
easy.explanation: God gives Assyria a charge to take the spoil, take the prey, and tread the people down.
easy.q: Why is Assyria sent against the sinful nation?

answers: As the result of his own strength and wisdom
easy.explanation: He says, “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom.”
easy.q: How does the king of Assyria view his accomplishments?

answers: God sends Assyria to punish, but Assyria intends to destroy many nations
God sends Assyria to save, but Assyria refuses
God sends Assyria to build, but Assyria farms
medium.explanation: Assyria is commissioned to punish one people, but its heart seeks to destroy and cut off many nations.
medium.q: What is the difference between God's purpose and Assyria's personal intention?

medium.explanation: The image of mire conveys severe oppression and humiliation.
medium.q: What does “to tread them down like the mire of the streets” communicate?

answers: Tools are stronger than their users
An instrument cannot boast over the one who uses it
medium.explanation: An axe cannot boast against the hewer, just as Assyria cannot claim independent credit for God's work.
medium.q: What does the illustration of the axe and the saw teach?

answers: It thinks its own power is the source of all its success
It thinks it has no army
It thinks the cities are too small
challenge.explanation: Assyria forgets that it is an instrument in God's hand and attributes everything to its own strength and wisdom.
challenge.q: What is the central error in Assyria's pride?

answers: It shows that Assyria conquered nothing
It presents its conquests as proof of superior power
It shows that all the cities were allies
challenge.explanation: Assyria names fallen cities and kingdoms as evidence of its supposed greatness.
challenge.q: How does Assyria's list of conquered cities support the theme of pride?

answers: The hewer does not need a tool
The instrument should not claim the work of its user
challenge.explanation: The rhetorical question denies Assyria the right to boast as though it acted by its own power.
challenge.q: What is the meaning of “Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith?”

paragraphs.title: Assyria's Downfall and the Return of Israel's Remnant

answers: It will be consumed by fire
easy.explanation: The Lord will kindle a burning that consumes Assyria's glory.
easy.q: What will happen to Assyria's glory?

answers: All the trees in their fullness
easy.explanation: The rest of the trees “shall be few, that a child may write them.”
easy.q: How many of the trees of Assyria's forest will remain?

answers: The Lord, the Holy One of Israel
easy.explanation: The remnant will no longer stay upon the one who smote them but will stay upon the Lord in truth.
easy.q: Upon whom will Israel's remnant rely?

medium.explanation: The forest represents Assyria's power and glory, which God will consume.
medium.q: What does the burning forest symbolize?

answers: All Israel will remain in captivity
The remnant will return to the mighty God
medium.explanation: The remnant of Jacob will return unto “the mighty God.”
medium.q: What does “the remnant shall return” mean in this context?

answers: It shifts from the Lord to Assyria
It shifts from foreign powers to genuine reliance on the Lord
It shifts from itself to earthly kings
medium.explanation: The remnant will no longer depend on the foreign power that struck it but on the Lord.
medium.q: What change takes place in the remnant's dependence?

answers: Both show a movement from trusting human power to trusting God
The remnant's return makes Assyria stronger
challenge.explanation: Assyria's fall removes false human security, while Israel's remnant returns to faithful dependence on God.
challenge.q: What relationship exists between Assyria's downfall and the remnant's return?

answers: It will be large and numerous
It will be so small that it can easily be counted
challenge.explanation: The number of remaining trees will be very small, easily counted even by a child.
challenge.q: What does “that a child may write them” suggest about the remnant of the forest?

answers: As a determined consumption in the midst of all the land
challenge.explanation: The Lord will make “a consumption, even determined, in the midst of all the land.”
challenge.q: How is judgment upon the land described?

paragraphs.title: Encouragement to Zion and the Breaking of Assyria's Yoke

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “O my people that dwellest in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian.”
easy.q: Who is told not to be afraid of the Assyrian?

answers: It will cease after a little while
It will be turned only against Israel
easy.explanation: The Lord promises, “For yet a very little while, and the indignation shall cease.”
easy.q: What will happen to the indignation?

answers: The burden and yoke of oppression
easy.explanation: The burden will be taken from the shoulder and the yoke from the neck.
easy.q: What will be removed from Israel?

answers: God will end His indignation and judge Assyria
medium.explanation: The Lord promises that His anger will cease and that He will raise a scourge against Assyria.
medium.q: Why does Zion not need to fear Assyria?

answers: His oppressive load or yoke will be removed
medium.explanation: The burden and yoke symbolize Assyria's oppressive rule over God's people.
medium.q: What does “his burden shall be taken away” mean?

answers: The rod represents oppression, and the yoke represents Assyria's rule
The rod is used to build Jerusalem
medium.explanation: The rod and staff picture Assyria's power, while the yoke represents the resulting bondage.
medium.q: What is the relationship between the rod and the yoke?

answers: The yoke will be broken through God's appointed power and blessing
The yoke is literally made of oil
challenge.explanation: The phrase points to the destruction of the oppressive yoke through the power associated with God's anointing.
challenge.q: What does “the yoke shall be destroyed because of the anointing” emphasize?

answers: It begins with fear and ends with Assyria's victory
It forbids fear and then promises the end of indignation and the breaking of the yoke
It begins with freedom and ends with Assyria's strengthening
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from “be not afraid” to the promises that God's anger will cease and the yoke will be destroyed.
challenge.q: How is the encouraging message structured?

challenge.explanation: The Lord promises to end the indignation and remove the burden and yoke.
challenge.q: Who initiates the change in Israel's condition?

paragraphs.title: Assyria's March toward Jerusalem and the Fall of the Forest

easy.explanation: The army advances through the surrounding settlements and reaches Nob, where it threatens Jerusalem.
easy.q: Toward what place is the Assyrian army advancing?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Ramah is afraid; Gibeah of Saul is fled,” and describes others gathering to flee.
easy.q: How do the settlements respond to the Assyrian advance?

answers: Cut it down and humble it
easy.explanation: The Lord will lop its boughs, hew down the high ones, and humble the haughty.
easy.q: What will the Lord do to Assyria's forest?

answers: It reaches a position from which Jerusalem is directly threatened
medium.explanation: At Nob, Assyria shakes its hand against the mount of the daughter of Zion and the hill of Jerusalem.
medium.q: What is significant about Assyria's arrival at Nob?

medium.explanation: To lop a bough is to cut or prune it, symbolizing the cutting down of Assyria's power.
medium.q: What does “lop the bough” mean in this passage?

answers: It shows Assyria's frightening advance followed by the humiliation of its power
It shows that Assyria never advances
It describes the planting of a forest
medium.explanation: The passage first depicts military fear and movement, then pictures God's judgment as the cutting down of a forest.
medium.q: How does the movement from the settlements to the forest image strengthen the message?

challenge.explanation: The lofty forest represents Assyria's strength, army, and pride, which God will bring down.
challenge.q: What does the forest symbolize at the end of the passage?

answers: Human fear of Assyria's power versus God's humbling of Assyria
challenge.explanation: Although the settlements fear the advancing army, the Lord will cut down and humble its power.
challenge.q: What is the central contrast in this passage?

answers: The powerful and proud will not remain invincible
The army will reach a higher place
challenge.explanation: The statement teaches that God will bring down those who are exalted and proud.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from “the high ones of stature shall be hewn down, and the haughty shall be humbled”?
